reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a crypto arbitrage process claiming an approximately 7x return from slightly more than $200 to $1,496. It instructs viewers to send $200 of MATIC to a contract for gas and call the flashloan function, creating a direct funding and participation flow tied to the promoted process. The risk disclaimer and lack of independently verified transactions do not remove the described combination of a high-return claim and funding instructions.

citations.quote: I create arbitrage videos using. Solid decode utilizing smart contracts specifically in this arbitrage I'm going to be utilizing smart. Contracts from Aave which are here in GitHub and from Uniswap and we're. Going to be using flash loans
On Deploy, Enter your token details and deploy the contract
Send $200 of MATIC to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
Call 'flashloan' function in Remix.
$10,000 for providing $200 worth of gas to this contract.

opening.argument: Judge, distinguish a claimed personal result from a promise to viewers. The creator says, “This worked for me. But TRY IT AT YOUR OWN RISK!” and qualifies the method’s longevity: “It probably won't work forever. Someone will shut it down.” Those warnings matter when interpreting the later account of a gain. The video may present a risky and unusually profitable experiment, but its own language does not promise that another viewer will reproduce the result.

citations.quote: This worked for me. But TRY IT AT YOUR OWN RISK!
It probably won't work forever. Someone will shut it down.
A little over $200 to $1,496. I just did a 7X.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening is right that viewers are told to fund a contract, but it treats that instruction and the reported return as though they amount to a promised payout. The description calls the transfer a “gas fee for all swaps,” while the speaker frames the result in the first person and expressly warns viewers of risk. Neither qualification proves the process works; both limit what can fairly be inferred about a guarantee to viewers.

citations.quote: Send $200 of MATIC to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
I just did a 7X.
But TRY IT AT YOUR OWN RISK!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The warning does not change the practical invitation. Viewers are told to “Send $200 of MATIC to the contract for gas fee for all swaps” and then to “Call 'flashloan' function in Remix.” The speaker pairs that funding sequence with “A little over $200 to $1,496. I just did a 7X.” Calling it a personal result avoids an explicit guarantee, but does not remove the promoted, high-return funded-contract process.

opening.argument: Judge, the organizing structure is a technical walkthrough. The speaker introduces “some educational information” for newcomers, explains that Remix is “an IDE to compile Solidity smart contracts online,” and walks through compiling and deploying a contract. The sampled screen also shows the Remix development interface. The gain is reported as part of the demonstration, but the observable teaching content is substantial. A tutorial can describe a risky transaction without its primary character becoming a solicitation.

it is an IDE to compile Solidity smart contracts online.
Create new file in Remix and paste Contract code and wait for everything to load, Go to Solidity Compiler and Select compiler to 0.5.0+commit version and hit Compile.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening isolates the funding and function-call steps, but those steps occur within a longer compiler-and-deployment walkthrough. The speaker describes the purpose of Remix and the description gives concrete setup instructions. That context does not verify the claimed profit, but it supports reading the video as a demonstration of a workflow rather than simply an appeal to send money.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A technical walkthrough can also be the vehicle for a funded-contract pitch. The instructions progress beyond compiling: viewers are directed to “Send $200 of MATIC to the contract for gas fee for all swaps” and “Call 'flashloan' function in Remix.” The speaker then reports “A little over $200 to $1,496. I just did a 7X.” Showing a development interface does not establish that the proposed mechanism produced that return.

citations.quote: Send $200 of MATIC to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
Call 'flashloan' function in Remix.
A little over $200 to $1,496. I just did a 7X.

opening.argument: Judge, the stated transaction is funding a contract the viewer deploys, not buying access to a seller’s investment account. The instructions say to enter token details and deploy the contract, then obtain “the Contract address from Remix”; they describe the MATIC transfer as covering swaps. The speaker likewise says, “we're going to create our own coin.” These sources do not identify a payee controlled by the presenter, a credential request, or a contractual promise of repayment. The reported return warrants skepticism, but the specified activity can also be read as a risky self-directed trading operation.

citations.quote: On Deploy, Enter your token details and deploy the contract
Get the Contract address from Remix
Send $200 of MATIC to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
we're going to create our own coin

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening establishes a funding step and an asserted high return, but not who controls the deployed contract or receives its funds. The stated sequence has viewers deploy a contract and retrieve its address from Remix before sending MATIC. That does not prove the contract is trustworthy; it does mean the funding instruction alone does not establish a transfer to the presenter.

citations.quote: On Deploy, Enter your token details and deploy the contract
Get the Contract address from Remix
Send $200 of MATIC to the contract for gas fee for all swaps

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of an identified presenter-controlled payee does not settle what the supplied contract does. The description directs viewers to copy contract code from a supplied link, deploy it, send it $200 of MATIC, and call its flashloan function. The speaker reports a 7X result, but the cited instructions do not independently verify the contract’s behavior or that return. This is still an actionable funded-contract process promoted through an extraordinary gain claim.
